promptText: In Spring AI, what is the key architectural difference between ChatModel and ChatClient?
options: ChatModel is the thin, portable interface for a raw request/response call; ChatClient is the fluent, higher-level API built on top of it that adds Advisors, memory, structured output, and prompt building
ChatModel only supports streaming responses, while ChatClient only supports synchronous responses
ChatClient is required for local models, while ChatModel is required for hosted provider APIs
ChatModel and ChatClient are two names for the exact same interface, kept for backward compatibility
explanation: ChatModel is intentionally minimal (Prompt in, ChatResponse out) and implemented consistently across providers, while ChatClient wraps a ChatModel and adds the ergonomics real applications need: an Advisor chain, structured output binding, and conversation memory.

promptText: A ChatClient call chains a MessageChatMemoryAdvisor before a QuestionAnswerAdvisor (RAG). What is the practical consequence of this ordering?
options: The retrieved RAG context ends up appended after conversation history in the assembled prompt, changing how the model weighs recency of history versus the retrieved facts
The RAG advisor will simply be skipped because memory advisors always run exclusively
Advisor order has no effect on the assembled prompt, only on which advisor's logs appear first
This ordering causes the ChatClient call to throw an exception at runtime
explanation: Advisors intercept and rewrite the request in the order they are chained, similar to a servlet filter chain; if memory runs before RAG, the retrieved context ends up positioned differently in the prompt than if RAG ran first, which changes how the model weighs recency versus retrieved grounding.

promptText: A service calls `chatClient.prompt().user(text).call().entity(TicketTriage.class)` where TicketTriage has a `priority` field. The call succeeds and deserializes without error, but returns `priority: 999`. What does this reveal about structured output binding?
options: Structured output binding guarantees syntactic/structural validity but not semantic correctness — a separate validation layer (bean validation, range checks) is still needed to catch nonsensical but well-typed values
This is impossible; successful deserialization always guarantees the value is semantically valid
The structured output converter should have retried automatically until a semantically valid value was produced
This indicates the ChatModel bean is misconfigured and should be replaced with a raw ChatModel call
explanation: Structural failures (invalid JSON, missing fields) are caught by the converter, but semantic failures (valid JSON, nonsensical values like priority 999) require an additional validation layer applied after successful deserialization.

promptText: A team switches a chat feature from a blocking call to `.stream()` with Server-Sent Events. What actually improves as a result?
options: Perceived latency — the user sees tokens as they're generated instead of waiting for the full response — while total generation time, token cost, and server throughput remain unchanged
Total wall-clock generation time, because streaming causes the model to generate tokens faster
Server-side request throughput, because streaming uses fewer server resources per request than a blocking call
The per-token cost charged by the model provider, since streamed tokens are billed at a discounted rate
explanation: Streaming is purely a perceived-latency/UX optimization: total generation time and cost are unchanged, and holding a connection open for the full stream duration can even tie up a connection slightly longer than an equivalent non-streamed call.

promptText: When configuring a retry policy for calls to a flaky model provider, which failure types should generally be retried, and which should never be retried?
options: Retry timeouts, 429s, and 5xx responses (often transient); never retry 400s or 401s (the request is inherently invalid and will fail identically again)
Retry every exception type uniformly, since LLM calls are inherently unreliable and any failure could be transient
Never retry any LLM call, since every retried attempt risks producing a different, non-deterministic answer
Retry only 400 and 401 errors, since those are the cheapest failures to reattempt
explanation: Rate-limit and server-side errors often reflect transient load and are reasonable to retry with backoff, but retrying a malformed request or an auth failure just repeats the identical failure while wasting a full, billable model invocation.

promptText: How should a unit test for a service that calls ChatClient typically be written?
options: Mock the ChatClient/ChatModel (or a narrow wrapping collaborator) so the test exercises the service's own logic — routing, error handling, response parsing — without a real, slow, non-deterministic, billable model call
Always call the real model with temperature 0, since that guarantees fully deterministic and reproducible unit test output
Unit tests should be skipped entirely for LLM-calling services since their behavior can never be verified without a live model
Mock only the vector store, since ChatClient itself cannot be mocked in a Spring Boot test
explanation: This mirrors the same discipline used for any external dependency like a repository: mocking the injected client lets the test verify the service's own orchestration logic quickly and deterministically, leaving real-model verification to a separate integration/regression suite.

promptText: What does a circuit breaker add on top of retry and timeout configuration for a model provider integration?
options: It tracks the aggregate failure rate across many requests and, once a threshold is crossed, fails fast or routes to a fallback for a cool-down period, instead of every individual request separately waiting out a timeout against a provider that has already demonstrated it isn't responding
It replaces the need for any timeout configuration, since a circuit breaker inherently bounds how long a single request can take
It guarantees that retried requests will always succeed on the second attempt
It only applies to database calls and has no meaningful use for LLM provider integrations
explanation: Retry and timeout handle one request's transient failure; a circuit breaker handles the aggregate pattern — once failure rate crosses a threshold it opens, avoiding the case where every request individually pays the full timeout-then-retry cost against a provider that is clearly down.

promptText: Why does idempotency matter more for a client retrying an LLM request than for a typical internal REST call retry?
options: The LLM call is non-deterministic (a retry can produce a different answer, not just a slower one) and every attempt is a full, separately billed model invocation, so a naive retry can both change the visible result and double the cost
LLM APIs do not support HTTP retries at the network level, so idempotency keys are required purely for transport compatibility
Idempotency only matters for LLM calls that use function/tool calling, and is irrelevant for plain text generation
Idempotency keys are needed because LLM providers cache responses server-side and always return stale data on retry otherwise
explanation: Unlike an idempotent GET, a temperature-driven LLM generation call can legitimately produce different output on retry and always costs a new billable invocation, so an idempotency-key pattern (cache or join an in-flight call) prevents both a visibly inconsistent result and duplicated cost or side effects.

promptText: A team swaps their EmbeddingModel bean to a newer, cheaper embedding provider to save cost, relying on Spring AI's provider-neutral VectorStore/EmbeddingModel abstraction. What does this abstraction NOT solve for them?
options: The need to re-embed and rebuild the index for the entire corpus, since vectors from two different embedding models are not comparable and a similarity search mixing them produces meaningless results
The need to update any application code, since the abstraction requires touching every call site that performs a similarity search
The requirement to migrate to a different VectorStore backend at the same time as switching embedding providers
The need to change the ChatClient's Advisor chain configuration
explanation: The provider-neutral interface makes swapping providers a configuration change for application code, but it cannot make two embedding models' vector spaces comparable — switching embedding models is always a data re-indexing exercise, not a transparent swap.

promptText: An integration test against a real (non-zero temperature) model fails intermittently even though nothing else changed, because the assertion checks the response text for exact string equality. What is the correct fix?
options: Reframe the assertion around stable properties — schema validity, required/forbidden keywords, or a semantic similarity threshold — rather than exact text matching, since a sampling model can legitimately vary its wording between runs
Retry the test up to 10 times and mark it passing if any single attempt matches the exact expected string
Conclude there is a genuine bug in the model provider's API and file a support ticket
Disable the test permanently, since real-model integration tests can never be made reliable
explanation: A model sampling at nonzero temperature can produce different, individually correct wording across runs, so exact-match assertions are inherently flaky; testing should check properties that are stable across acceptable variation, such as schema conformance or required content.

promptText: Why is caching a full generated LLM response riskier than caching a typical piece of application data, such as a computed report?
options: A stale cached LLM answer reads as a fully formed, confident response identical in appearance to a fresh, correct one, so there is no visible signal to a user or naive monitoring that the content is now wrong because the underlying facts changed
LLM responses cannot technically be serialized into a cache store due to their unstructured text format
Caching LLM responses is actually safer than caching other data because generated text never depends on external facts
LLM response caches always expire automatically the instant the underlying source document changes, unlike other caches
explanation: Unlike a stale cached price that might visibly mismatch elsewhere on a page, a stale cached LLM answer has the same tone, format, and confidence as a fresh one, so TTLs need to be tied explicitly to how fast the underlying facts can change, or invalidation tied to source-document updates.

promptText: An LLM-calling service autoscales based on CPU utilization, but fails to scale up during a real traffic spike even as request queues grow and latency climbs. What is the most likely diagnosis and correct fix?
options: CPU/memory is the wrong signal because the bottleneck is waiting on an external, rate-limited provider call, not local compute; autoscaling should instead be driven by queue depth, in-flight request count, or latency — and if the true bottleneck is the provider's own rate limit, adding instances won't help at all
The service needs a larger CPU-based scaling threshold, since the current threshold is simply set too high
This indicates a memory leak in the JVM that must be fixed with a heap dump before autoscaling can work correctly
Autoscaling should be disabled entirely for any service that calls an external LLM provider
explanation: CPU/memory during an LLM call is typically minimal since the thread is mostly waiting on a network response, so CPU-based autoscaling never detects the real bottleneck; and once the provider's own account-level rate limit is the binding constraint, more instances share the same fixed quota and don't help at all.

promptText: A service's circuit breaker opens for its primary model provider and automatically routes traffic to a secondary fallback provider. A week later, a report surfaces that structured-output parsing failures spiked specifically during that fallback window, even though the fallback provider was 'up' the whole time. What does this reveal about fallback design?
options: A fallback model is rarely a perfect drop-in replacement — it can differ in structured-output reliability or instruction-following strictness, so fallback paths need to be tested with the same prompt templates and schemas used against the primary, and periodically exercised deliberately rather than trusted blindly when rarely used
This proves the circuit breaker itself is malfunctioning and should be replaced with a simple retry loop
Structured-output parsing failures are always caused by the primary provider's outage propagating into the fallback provider's responses
Fallback providers should never be used for any request that requires structured output, under any circumstances
explanation: Different providers or model tiers can differ meaningfully in structured-output reliability even while otherwise healthy; a fallback path needs to be validated against the same schemas as the primary and periodically exercised (a scheduled canary or partial live traffic) so a silently broken or weaker fallback isn't discovered only during a real incident.

promptText: A prompt change intended to make an assistant's tone warmer improves the aggregate golden-dataset score in CI, and the team ships it. Which testing gap does this scenario illustrate, and what would have caught the actual regression?
options: An aggregate-only score can mask a category-specific regression (here, refusals of out-of-scope requests becoming less firm); the CI gate needs per-category score breakdowns, not just the overall average, to catch a regression concentrated in one input category
The golden dataset itself was too small and simply needed more examples of the same category that was already passing
This proves LLM-as-judge scoring should never be used for tone-related evaluation criteria under any circumstances
Aggregate scores are always sufficient as long as the golden dataset includes at least 100 examples
explanation: A prompt change can improve the common case while quietly regressing a rare-but-important category (like firmly declining out-of-scope requests); regression gates need to check per-category scores specifically, since an aggregate-only check can pass a change that ships a real, category-concentrated regression.

promptText: A RAG feature's golden-dataset CI evaluation uses a single LLM-judge score of 'rate this answer 1-10' and shows improvement after a prompt change that made answers noticeably longer. A parallel human spot-check finds the longer answers are not actually more accurate. What combination of concepts explains this, and what is the correct fix that also connects to separating RAG failure modes?
options: LLM-judges have a documented bias toward longer, more confident-sounding answers regardless of correctness; the fix is a narrower, criteria-specific rubric (e.g., does it state the correct fact) validated periodically against human review, and evaluating retrieval and generation/faithfulness as separate metrics so a generation-side scoring artifact isn't mistaken for a genuine retrieval or overall quality improvement
The result proves LLM-judges are strictly unusable for any RAG evaluation and must be replaced entirely by manual human review for every single request
The longer answers are objectively better because higher token count always correlates with higher information density in generated text
This is expected and requires no fix, since golden-dataset scores are inherently more reliable than human judgment in every case
explanation: LLM-judges can systematically favor longer, more assertive answers independent of actual correctness; narrowing the rubric to specific, checkable criteria and periodically validating judge scores against human review corrects this, and keeping retrieval metrics separate from generation/faithfulness metrics prevents a generation-side scoring bias from being misread as a broader quality or retrieval improvement.
